analysis.one_liner: Creates a USDA office to investigate and prosecute big meatpackers for anticompetitive practices.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to create a USDA special investigator for meatpacker competition died without a vote in the 118th Congress, despite 11 senators signing on.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of the Special Investigator for Competition Matters inside the Department of Agriculture. It would use subpoenas to investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act by large meatpackers and poultry dealers, and could bring civil and administrative cases against them directly. It was introduced by a Democrat and a group of bipartisan cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, and was never brought to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers, hog farmers, and contract poultry growers who say large meatpackers pay them unfairly low prices and use opaque pricing systems. Shoppers would also benefit if tougher enforcement lowers meat prices; a handful of big companies process most of the country's beef, pork, and poultry, which economists link to higher prices at the grocery store.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ranchers, poultry growers, and grocery shoppers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a dedicated USDA office headed by a senior career employee to investigate and prosecute violations of the Packers and Stockyards Act by packers and live poultry dealers.
Gives the office authority to use all available tools, including subpoenas, and to bring civil or administrative actions directly against packers and live poultry dealers.
Makes the office a liaison to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission on competition in the food and agriculture sector, and to Homeland Security on food-supply security.
Requires a staff of attorneys and professionals with appropriate expertise, coordinating with USDA's general counsel and the Packers and Stockyards Division.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking and poultry companies, which would face a dedicated investigator with subpoena power focused on their pricing and contracting practices. Taxpayers fund the new office, a modest cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates an enforcement office but does not change market structure: it cannot break up companies or rewrite the rules that let four firms dominate meat processing, so it treats symptoms of consolidation rather than its causes.

The new office's scope is limited to entities already regulated under the Packers and Stockyards Act, and its cases could overlap with the Justice Department and FTC, raising questions about duplication.
The Packers and Stockyards Act dates to 1921, and enforcement under it has historically been slow, so a new office is no guarantee that enforcement actually gets faster or tougher.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct cost is small: one new office with a professional staff inside USDA. The potential benefit to ranchers facing unfair pricing and to consumers facing high meat prices is real but not guaranteed, because the office only enforces an existing 1921 law and cannot by itself change how concentrated the meatpacking industry has become. It is a modest enforcement upgrade, not a structural fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with bipartisan support and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never brought it to a vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jon Tester introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, joined by ten cosponsors from both parties.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The Agriculture Committee took no further action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed in that committee.
More than a year later, in May 2024, the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee held a hearing at which the bill was discussed, but the bill itself still received no vote.
The bill never reached the Senate floor and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers and poultry companies are better off: the dedicated USDA investigator with subpoena power who would have pursued their pricing and contracting practices was never created. Ranchers and shoppers are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large meatpackers who avoided new scrutiny

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create the USDA special investigator for meatpacker competition.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as one of four Republican cosponsors, adding bipartisan weight.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Booker, Klobuchar, Stabenow, Wyden, Heinrich, Rounds, Daines, and Hoeven
for.what_they_did: Signed onto the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship across the Senate.

against.name: Senate Agriculture Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Debbie Stabenow (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, held no hearing, markup, or vote on it, and never advanced it to the floor despite the chair being one of its cosponsors.

against.name: Meatpacking and poultry industry interests
against.role: Companies that would face the new investigator
against.what_they_did: Faced creation of a dedicated USDA enforcement office with subpoena power over their sector; opposition to a stronger special investigator in the meat industry was widely reported during the debate.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 initial sponsors were bipartisan (6 Democrats and 4 Republicans plus sponsor Tester), so the bill did not fail on party grounds; it stalled inside a committee without a vote.

industries.note: A handful of firms process most U.S. beef, pork, and chicken, and the bill would give a dedicated USDA office subpoena power and standing to sue them over anticompetitive pricing and contracting. Their interest in avoiding this enforcement runs against ranchers' pay and shoppers' prices.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and contract poultry growers
industries.note: Stronger Packers and Stockyards enforcement is aimed at the unfair pricing and contract practices growers say big packers use against them, which is why farm-state senators from both parties backed the bill.
